summary: This document consolidates the iSCSI protocol, a transport for SCSI that runs over TCP and aims to comply with SCSI Architecture Model SAM-2. RFC 3720 defined the original protocol, and later RFCs, including 3721 and 3980, added to it. This document brings it together in one place.

eli5.summary: Disk commands normally travel on a short cable inside a computer. iSCSI packs them to travel across a network so a faraway disk acts like it is next door.

questions: what is an iscsi qualified name
subtitle: How SCSI storage commands travel over ordinary TCP/IP networks, all consolidated into a single specification.

tldr.problem: SCSI, the family of protocols for talking to disks and other I/O devices, had been mapped only to I/O-specific transports with limited distance. The Internet had no standard way to carry SCSI.
tldr.mechanism: iSCSI wraps SCSI commands, data and status in iSCSI Protocol Data Units (PDUs) that travel over one or more TCP connections grouped into a session. A Login Phase authenticates the parties and negotiates parameters before any SCSI command is sent.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7143 merges RFCs 3720, 3980, 4850 and 5048 into one document and obsoletes them, and it updates RFC 3721. Its text wins wherever the older RFCs differ in meaning.

today: RFC 7143 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2014. It obsoletes RFC 3720, RFC 3980, RFC 4850 and RFC 5048, updates RFC 3721, and is not itself obsoleted or updated by any later RFC listed in its metadata.

sections.title: Why iSCSI Exists
sections.content:
The Small Computer System Interface (SCSI) is a family of protocols for communicating with I/O devices, especially storage. It is a client-server design. Clients are called initiators. They send SCSI commands to logical units (LUs), the parts of a server called a target. A SCSI transport maps this exchange onto a particular interconnect.

SCSI had been mapped to Parallel SCSI, IPI, IEEE 1394 (FireWire) and Fibre Channel. The RFC describes these as I/O-specific transports with limited distance. iSCSI instead carries SCSI over TCP/IP, which lets it use existing Internet infrastructure and management facilities and removes the distance limit. It aims to comply fully with the SCSI Architecture Model, SAM-2.

RFC 7143 is a consolidated edition. RFC 3720 defined the original protocol, RFC 3721 covers naming examples and discovery, and RFCs 3980, 4850 and 5048 added a naming format, a public extension key and a set of corrections.
sections.eli5: Long ago, a computer talked to its disk through a short cable. iSCSI lets the computer send the very same requests through the network, like using a phone line instead of shouting across the room.

sections.title: Sessions, Connections and Numbering
sections.content:
The RFC describes two layers. The SCSI layer builds and receives SCSI command descriptor blocks (CDBs). The iSCSI layer builds and receives iSCSI PDUs and relays them over one or more TCP connections. The group of TCP connections linking an initiator with a target is a session, which is equivalent to a SCSI I_T nexus. Connections can be added to and removed from a session, and each one has a connection ID (CID). Across all connections the initiator sees one "target image". Implementations MUST support at least one connection per session and MAY support several.

Ordering relies on three kinds of numbers. The CmdSN numbers commands session-wide and gives ordered delivery across connections. Status numbering (StatSN) is per connection and helps detect missing status. Data sequencing (DataSN, R2TSN) is per command and detects missing data. The CmdSN is a 32-bit counter compared with Serial Number Arithmetic from RFC 1982.

Flow control uses a window. The target advertises ExpCmdSN, the next command it expects, and MaxCmdSN, the highest it will accept. The queuing capacity is MaxCmdSN - ExpCmdSN + 1, and the target MUST silently ignore a non-immediate command outside that range. Commands marked immediate carry the current CmdSN without advancing it and may lie outside the window.

One more rule shapes everything: command connection allegiance. The response, data and R2T for a command MUST travel on the same TCP connection that carried the command, unless allegiance is explicitly reassigned during recovery.
sections.eli5: Think of a restaurant with several waiters (connections) serving one table (session). Every order gets a number so the kitchen cooks in order, and the waiter who took an order brings back that dish.

sections.title: iSCSI Names and Portals
sections.content:
Every iSCSI node, whether initiator, target or both, MUST have an iSCSI name. Names are globally unique, permanent, and do not imply a location, so a node can move or have several addresses without changing its name. A name names a logical software entity, not a network card. Implementations MUST accept names up to 223 bytes. A name is UTF-8 text in Normalization Form C, using dash, dot and colon for formatting, and uppercase characters are prohibited.

A name has a type designator and a unique string. Three formats exist: iqn. (a date code in yyyy-mm form plus a reversed domain name, with an optional colon-prefixed string), eui. (an IEEE EUI-64 identifier as 16 hexadecimal digits) and naa. (a Network Address Authority identifier in hexadecimal). An example from the RFC is iqn.2001-04.com.example:storage:diskarrays-sn-a8675309.

On the network side, a Network Portal is a TCP/IP address (and, for a target, a listening TCP port). Portals are gathered into portal groups identified by a Portal Group Tag between 0 and 65535. A SCSI initiator port maps to the initiator name plus the ISID, and a SCSI target port maps to the target name plus the portal group tag. A target assigns a non-zero TSIH at session creation, and the ISID RULE allows only one session with a given ISID between an initiator and a target portal group.

Initiators can discover targets with the SendTargets text request, and equipment needing more SHOULD implement iSNS (RFC 4171). The RFC says implementations SHOULD NOT rely on SLP-based discovery.
sections.eli5: An iSCSI name is like a person's full name, which stays the same even if they move house. The address (portal) is where they live today, and it can change.

sections.title: The iSCSI PDU and Its Header
sections.content:
All iSCSI messages are PDUs. Each starts with a fixed 48-byte Basic Header Segment (BHS). It MAY be followed by Additional Header Segments (AHS), a header digest, a data segment and a data digest. Every segment starts on a 4-byte boundary, so padding runs from 0 to 3 bytes and SHOULD be sent as zero. Response PDUs have no AHS.

The Opcode and DataSegmentLength appear in every PDU, and the Initiator Task Tag and LUN always sit in the same place. The I bit marks a request for immediate delivery, and the F bit marks the final PDU of a sequence. DataSegmentLength excludes padding, and digests are not included in length fields. The initiator assigns a task tag to each task, unique session-wide, and the value 0xffffffff is reserved.

The RFC defines these request and response types: SCSI Command and SCSI Response, Task Management Function Request and Response, SCSI Data-Out and Data-In, Ready To Transfer (R2T), Asynchronous Message, Text Request and Response, Login Request and Response, Logout Request and Response, SNACK Request, Reject, and NOP-Out and NOP-In. The SCSI Command PDU carries the CDB, the CmdSN, the ExpStatSN and an Expected Data Transfer Length. Its R and W flags show whether data is expected to be read or written.
sections.eli5: Every iSCSI message has a label on the front, always the same size, saying what kind of message it is and how long the rest is. Extra pages are added behind the label when needed.

sections.title: Moving Data: Commands, R2T and Data PDUs
sections.content:
Once in the Full Feature Phase, the initiator encapsulates SCSI commands in iSCSI PDUs. Data going from the initiator to the target (a write) is solicited when it answers an R2T (Ready To Transfer), or unsolicited when sent without one. The R2T tells the initiator the buffer offset and length the target wants. It carries a Target Transfer Tag that the initiator copies into the matching Data-Out PDUs. The Desired Data Transfer Length MUST NOT be 0 and MUST NOT exceed MaxBurstLength.

Unsolicited data can ride inside the command PDU as immediate data or follow as separate Data-Out PDUs, up to FirstBurstLength. Anything beyond that MUST be solicited. The keys InitialR2T and ImmediateData decide which forms are allowed. A read needs no R2T: the target sends Data-In PDUs, and the last one may also carry the status when there is no exception. The target may also send several R2Ts at once, limited by MaxOutstandingR2T.

Data PDUs carry a DataSN, and R2Ts an R2TSN, so a missing PDU can be spotted. An end-of-sequence is signaled by the F bit. The RFC also describes task management: functions such as ABORT TASK, LOGICAL UNIT RESET and TASK REASSIGN let an initiator control tasks. It also defines a FastAbort multi-task abort mode, selected through the TaskReporting key.
sections.eli5: Writing to a disk is like asking a teacher if you may hand in your homework. Usually the teacher says "ready, send page one" first. If you both agree, you can slip the first pages in with your request to save time.

sections.title: The Login Phase
sections.content:
Login sets up a TCP connection for iSCSI use, authenticates the parties, negotiates parameters and ties the connection to a session. Targets listen on a well-known TCP port, and the initiator connects to it. Until login ends, only Login Request and Login Response PDUs are allowed. A target that receives any other PDU before the Login Phase starts MUST terminate the connection.

Login has two optional stages: SecurityNegotiation and LoginOperationalNegotiation. At least one MUST be present, and security comes first. The initiator sets the T (Transit) bit to ask to move on, the CSG field names the current stage, and the NSG field names the next. The target agrees by answering with T set. The final accepting response must be to a request with T set and NSG at FullFeaturePhase. The first Login Request of every connection MUST include the InitiatorName, and non-Discovery sessions also need the TargetName.

What the target does with a login depends on the ISID and TSIH the initiator presents. A new ISID with TSIH zero creates a new session. An existing ISID with TSIH zero causes session reinstatement. An existing ISID with an existing non-zero TSIH and a new CID adds a connection, and with an existing CID it reinstates that connection. A non-zero TSIH with a new ISID fails the login. Login responses carry a status class and detail, for example 0201 for authentication failure.

There are two session types. A normal session is unrestricted. A Discovery session accepts only a Text Request with SendTargets and a Logout Request with reason "close the session". Logout PDUs close connections in an orderly way, and the Logout Response reports Time2Wait and Time2Retain for recovery.
sections.eli5: Login is like showing your ticket at a theater door. You prove who you are, agree on the rules, and only then are you let in to start watching the show.

sections.title: Key=Value Negotiation and Parameters
sections.content:
Parameters are exchanged as simple key=value text in the data segment of Login and Text PDUs. A key is either declarative, where one side just states a value, or negotiated, where a proposer offers a value or list and the acceptor selects. The acceptor may answer with the selected value, NotUnderstood, Irrelevant or Reject. Negotiations are explicit and atomic. A sender SHOULD allow at least six exchanges before giving up. The C (Continue) bit lets a value span several PDUs.

Many keys use a result function. For example InitialR2T uses OR with default Yes, and ImmediateData uses AND with default Yes. Others take the minimum. The RFC states these defaults:

  • MaxRecvDataSegmentLength: 8192 bytes
  • MaxBurstLength: 262144 (256 KB)
  • FirstBurstLength: 65536 (64 KB), which MUST NOT exceed MaxBurstLength
  • MaxOutstandingR2T: 1
  • DefaultTime2Wait: 2 seconds, and DefaultTime2Retain: 20 seconds
  • ErrorRecoveryLevel: 0

Optional digests protect integrity beyond what lower layers provide. HeaderDigest and DataDigest default to None, and CRC32C MUST be implemented by every initiator and target. The RFC says private keys use an X- prefix followed by a reversed domain name, and public keys are registered with IANA. The new public keys MUST NOT start with X#.
sections.eli5: Before playing a game, two friends agree on the rules by trading offers: "I want to play five rounds." "Let's do three." They keep the rules both can live with.

sections.title: Error Handling and Recovery
sections.content:
Two things motivate the recovery design. A PDU may fail its digest check and be dropped even though TCP delivered it, and a TCP connection may fail at any time. Active tasks should optionally be able to continue on another connection in the same session. Implementations have wide latitude about how much recovery to support, so long as the externally visible behavior is interoperable.

The RFC defines four recovery classes of increasing scope: within a command, within a connection, connection recovery and session recovery. They are bundled into three ErrorRecoveryLevel values, and the lower of the two values exchanged is the operational one.

The initiator toolkit includes NOP-Out probes, command retry, SNACK requests for retransmission of status, data or R2T, and TASK REASSIGN to move a command to a new connection. The target toolkit includes NOP-In probes, recovery R2T and SNACK support. Session recovery should be used when other attempts have failed. The RFC adds that very simple implementations MAY use session recovery on every iSCSI error.
sections.eli5: If one letter gets lost, you ask for just that letter again. If a whole road closes, you take another road. Only if everything goes wrong do you start the whole trip over.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The RFC notes that storage protocols historically had no need for security because devices were directly attached or on a separate storage network. Over IP, iSCSI must defend against active and passive attacks. It SHOULD NOT be run without in-band authentication, except in closed environments with very limited, well-controlled risk.

Two mechanisms complement each other. In-band authentication happens during login. The AuthMethod key can list KRB5, SRP, CHAP or None. All implementations MUST implement CHAP, and the other methods are optional. Methods that use cleartext passwords MUST NOT be used. IPsec protects packets at the IP level and is optional to use but mandatory to implement. After login, if IPsec is not used, PDUs travel in the clear.

For CHAP, implementations MUST support random secrets of up to 128 bits. If a secret has fewer than 96 random bits, IPsec encryption MUST be enforced. A CHAP secret used for one direction MUST NOT be used for the other, which blocks a reflection attack described in the text. The SRP prime modulus MUST be at least 768 bits. For IPsec, implementations MUST support IPsec v2 with ESPv2 in tunnel mode and SHOULD support IPsec v3. Those capable of 1 gigabit/second or higher MUST implement extended (64-bit) ESP sequence numbers. The text also says that replacing CHAP with a better method is anticipated in a future version of iSCSI.
sections.eli5: Locking your door is good, and checking who is knocking is good too. iSCSI offers both: it asks for a secret password, and it can put the whole conversation into a locked tube.

sections.title: What the Consolidation Changed
sections.content:
Besides merging the earlier RFCs, RFC 7143 makes changes. The most visible are listed in its summary of changes.

  • It sets iSCSIProtocolLevel to 1 and adds a normative reference to RFC 7144.
  • It removes markers and their keys, and removes SPKM authentication. A new section covers how to answer obsoleted keys: IFMarker and OFMarker get Reject (or No), never NotUnderstood.
  • It explicitly allows combined initiator-plus-target implementations, and requires that such a node use the same name for both roles.
  • FastAbort changes from a MUST to a SHOULD.
  • It requires IPsec v2 and recommends IPsec v3, and aligns the text with RFC 7146.
  • It prohibits the X#, Y# and Z# prefixes for new public keys, digests and authentication methods.
  • It adds UML diagrams and a Kerberos considerations section, and states that Appendix C on SendTargets is normative.
sections.eli5: This is like gathering five old rulebooks into one new, tidied-up book. A few rules were changed, a few dropped, and the new book wins whenever it disagrees with the old ones.
